reference.source: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Caused by gain-of-function mutations in FGFR2 and inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with variable expressivity
The cardinal feature is craniosynostosis (commonly bicoronal) with midface hypoplasia, shallow orbits and marked proptosis, but crucially the hands and feet are normal
Normal digits are the key point distinguishing Crouzon from Apert and Pfeiffer syndromes
Shallow orbits cause exorbitism that can threaten the globe, and strabismus and exposure keratopathy are common
Midface retrusion produces a relatively prominent lower jaw appearance, dental crowding, and airway narrowing with sleep-disordered breathing
A distinct allelic variant with acanthosis nigricans is caused by a specific FGFR3 mutation (Crouzon syndrome with acanthosis nigricans)
Raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus and Chiari-type hindbrain herniation may develop and warrant surveillance
Care is delivered by a craniofacial team using staged vault expansion and midface advancement, with orbital protection as a priority
reference.pathophysiology: Crouzon syndrome arises from activating mutations in fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2) that heighten receptor signalling in cranial suture mesenchyme. Overactive signalling accelerates osteoblast differentiation and premature ossification, so the calvarial sutures and cranial base synchondroses fuse early. This restricts the growth of the skull and, importantly, the midface, producing shallow orbits, proptosis and maxillary retrusion, while limb development is spared. An allelic form linked to an FGFR3 mutation additionally shows acanthosis nigricans.
additionalDifferentials: Pfeiffer syndrome (broad thumbs and great toes)
additionalInvestigations: FGFR2 molecular testing (with FGFR3 analysis if acanthosis nigricans is present)
Three-dimensional cranial CT to define fused sutures and orbital depth
MRI of the brain and craniocervical junction to assess ventricles and hindbrain herniation
Ophthalmology assessment for proptosis, corneal exposure and papilloedema
Sleep study and airway evaluation for obstructive sleep apnoea
Audiology assessment because conductive hearing loss is common
redFlags: Globe subluxation or corneal ulceration from severe exorbitism
Papilloedema or other signs of raised intracranial pressure
Progressive hydrocephalus or symptomatic Chiari malformation
Severe obstructive sleep apnoea causing hypoxia
reference.prognosis: Cognition is usually normal, and with timely craniofacial and neurosurgical management most children do well, but ongoing surveillance for raised intracranial pressure, visual and airway complications is essential throughout growth.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis because intelligence and limbs are normal
Failing to protect the exposed globe in a child with marked proptosis
Missing evolving hydrocephalus or hindbrain herniation on follow-up
Not screening for hearing loss and treating it, which can compound developmental delay
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Perform cranial vault expansion surgery for craniosynostosis to relieve raised intracranial pressure and permit brain growth
Undertake midface advancement, for example Le Fort III or monobloc osteotomy with distraction osteogenesis, to correct midface hypoplasia, protect the globes and improve the airway
Protect the eyes from exorbitism and exposure keratopathy with ocular lubrication, tarsorrhaphy or orbital decompression, and monitor for optic disc swelling
Manage obstructive sleep apnoea and airway narrowing with adenotonsillectomy, continuous positive airway pressure or tracheostomy in severe cases
Undertake neurosurgical surveillance for raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus and hindbrain herniation, with cerebrospinal fluid diversion where indicated
Assess hearing and manage conductive loss, and provide dental and orthodontic care for malocclusion
Provide genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant FGFR2 disorder with family testing, and coordinate care through a craniofacial multidisciplinary team
